annotation: The model treated the filer as a qualifying surviving spouse and used joint Social Security thresholds, reducing taxable Social Security to $11,542 instead of $18,542.70. It then used a joint standard deduction rather than the traced $18,341.33 itemized deduction plus $6,000 senior deduction.

The model incorrectly included $48,000 of tax-exempt veterans benefits, treated ESI premiums as an AGI adjustment despite no wages, and then contradicted its own positive taxable-income calculations by declaring the tax zero. The traced AGI and deductions leave $26,095.78 taxable, not zero.

The model treated the full 85% cap, $22,182, as taxable Social Security instead of applying the single-filer inclusion formula that yields $18,542.70. It also selected an estimated aged standard deduction rather than $18,341.33 of itemized deductions before the $6,000 senior deduction.

The model assigned qualifying-surviving-spouse status without a qualifying child, used joint Social Security thresholds and deductions, and then asserted that roughly $14,000 of taxable income generated no tax. The filer is taxed under the single pathway, with $26,095.78 of taxable income.

The model first derived tax near $3,300 from its own inputs, then submitted $1,176 without any computation producing that number. It also used the 85% Social Security cap and an estimated standard deduction instead of $18,542.70 of taxable Social Security and the traced itemized-plus-senior deductions.

The model assumed qualifying-surviving-spouse status and applied joint Social Security thresholds, a joint standard deduction, and joint brackets. The single-filer calculation instead includes $18,542.70 of Social Security and uses $18,341.33 of itemized deductions plus the $6,000 senior deduction.

The model used qualifying-surviving-spouse thresholds and deductions, then submitted $3,204 even though its stated $20,226 taxable income at a 10% rate produces $2,023. The applicable single-filer computation taxes $26,095.78 under the 2026 brackets.

The model included $22,182 of Social Security rather than $18,542.70 and omitted the separate $6,000 senior deduction. It also chose a $17,350 standard deduction instead of the traced $18,341.33 itemized deduction.

The model incorrectly assumed a TCJA sunset, introduced a personal exemption and pre-TCJA brackets, and treated ESI premiums as deductible medical expenses. The 2026 computation instead applies $18,341.33 of itemized deductions plus the $6,000 senior deduction and the operative 2026 brackets.

The stated $37,990 taxable income does not produce the submitted $1,109 under the applicable brackets. The traced deductions reduce AGI of $50,437.11 to $26,095.78 of taxable income, whose tax is $2,883.49.

The model applied an obsolete personal exemption and pre-TCJA 10% and 15% brackets while omitting the $6,000 senior deduction. The operative deductions total $24,341.33 and the operative 2026 brackets apply to $26,095.78.

The model assumed reverted pre-TCJA rules, subtracting a personal exemption and using 10% and 15% brackets while omitting the $6,000 senior deduction. The traced deduction is $18,341.33 itemized plus $6,000, followed by the operative 2026 brackets.

The model subtracted property taxes and a personal exemption under an obsolete sunset framework but omitted the $6,000 senior deduction. The correct deduction sequence leaves $26,095.78 taxable and produces $2,883.49 under the operative brackets.
The model used a personal exemption and pre-TCJA 10% and 15% brackets while failing to apply the separate $6,000 senior deduction. The operative itemized-plus-senior deductions total $24,341.33.

The model correctly followed the single-filer Social Security formula but imposed a $10,000 SALT cap and selected a $17,510 standard deduction. The traced itemized deduction is $18,341.33, and the additional $6,000 senior deduction reduces taxable income to $26,095.78.

The model asserted that age and surviving-spouse deductions eliminated taxable income without calculating them. The traced deductions total $24,341.33 against AGI of $50,437.11, leaving $26,095.78 taxable.

The model treated the aged standard deduction as large enough to offset pension, IRA, interest, and taxable Social Security income. AGI exceeds the traced $24,341.33 deductions by $26,095.78, so taxable income is not zero.

The model used joint surviving-spouse Social Security thresholds, producing $11,542 of taxable benefits, and subtracted a joint standard deduction. The single-filer formula produces $18,542.70 of taxable Social Security, followed by $18,341.33 itemized and $6,000 senior deductions.

The model approximated taxable Social Security and the aged deduction rather than carrying the traced amounts. AGI is $50,437.11 and total deductions are $24,341.33, leaving $26,095.78 rather than $26,336 taxable.

The model used a $24,150 standard-plus-age-plus-senior deduction instead of the traced $24,341.33 itemized-plus-senior deduction. That $191.33 deduction difference, together with the omitted $1.11 of AGI, caused its taxable income and tax to be too high.

The model's $359 answer reflects a joint surviving-spouse deduction and low-bracket treatment that nearly eliminates taxable income. The single-filer pathway leaves $26,095.78 taxable after the itemized and senior deductions.

The model asserted that standard and senior provisions exceeded taxable income without computing AGI or deductions. The traced $24,341.33 deductions do not offset $50,437.11 of AGI, leaving $26,095.78 taxable.

The model combined a single-level deduction with qualifying-surviving-spouse labeling, inserted a personal exemption, and applied obsolete 10% and 15% brackets. The operative calculation uses $24,341.33 of deductions and the 2026 single-filer brackets on $26,095.78.

The model assumed restored pre-TCJA law, subtracting a personal exemption and applying 10% and 15% brackets while omitting the $6,000 senior deduction. The operative deductions are $18,341.33 itemized plus $6,000.

The model incorrectly deducted ESI premiums as medical expenses, assumed a TCJA sunset and uncapped property taxes, and omitted the $6,000 senior deduction. It then used obsolete 10% and 15% brackets instead of the operative 2026 schedule.

The model used an $18,150 aged standard deduction plus $6,000 rather than the traced $18,341.33 itemized deduction plus $6,000. This understated deductions by $191.33 and overstated taxable income and tax.
The model returned no parseable value or explanation for the requested output.

The model selected a $24,150 standard-plus-age-plus-senior deduction rather than the traced $24,341.33 itemized-plus-senior deduction. The correct deduction choice leaves $26,095.78 taxable, not $26,286.

The model claimed the aged deduction eliminated tax and then subtracted a $750 elderly credit despite also describing income above that credit's usable range. The traced deductions leave $26,095.78 taxable, and no nonrefundable credit reduces the resulting $2,883.49 liability.

The model omitted taxable Social Security entirely even though provisional income includes tax-exempt interest and half the benefits and exceeds the applicable threshold. The inclusion is $18,542.70, and the model also incorrectly used a qualifying-surviving-spouse standard deduction.
The model asserted that the aged single standard deduction eliminated all taxable income. The traced $24,341.33 deductions leave $26,095.78 taxable from AGI of $50,437.11.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

The model treated age 77 and an asserted income exclusion calculation as sufficient for Texas aged Medicaid without identifying or satisfying an aged eligibility pathway. The person qualifies through no Medicaid category and receives no SSI, so the claimed below-threshold aged eligibility does not apply.

The model correctly stated that no earned wages were reported and that payroll tax therefore equals zero, but then submitted $1,534 instead. Its numeric output contradicts its own payroll-tax-base analysis and the required final-value contract.
The model returned no payroll_tax value or explanation, so the required output was missing.

The model incorrectly assumed the TCJA individual provisions expired and used a $15,150 base standard deduction supplemented by personal exemptions. The applicable 2026 joint standard deduction exceeds the household’s $31,402.21 AGI, leaving zero taxable income rather than $3,052.25.

The model used an obsolete post-TCJA-sunset structure consisting of a $19,600 standard deduction plus $10,000 of personal exemptions. The applicable 2026 joint standard deduction alone eliminates the household’s $31,402.21 AGI, so its $1,802.25 taxable-income calculation is erroneous.

The model both applied an obsolete projected post-TCJA-sunset standard deduction and miscomputed taxable Social Security as $11,588 instead of approximately $2,338.21. Those errors inflated AGI from $31,402.21 to $40,652 and created $20,252 of taxable income where the applicable 2026 joint standard deduction produces zero.

The model treated Social Security as largely excluded and invoked unspecified earned-income disregards and a medically needy spend-down despite the prompt listing no qualifying spend-down expenses. It also conflated QMB/SLMB assistance with Medicaid eligibility; the head fails the SSI-related income-and-asset tests and has no Medicaid category.

The model converted age-based potential eligibility into actual Medicaid eligibility without applying any category's financial tests. At 2.05 times FPL the head fails the MAGI categories, and the household does not satisfy the SSI-related pathway, leaving the Medicaid category as NONE.

The model incorrectly treated assumed Medicare Savings Program status as establishing Medicaid eligibility and never applied the SSI-related financial tests. The head qualifies for no Medicaid category: MAGI is 2.05 times FPL, and the aged SSI pathway's income-and-asset requirements are not met.
The model correctly computed Social Security tax of $1,801.968 and Medicare tax of $421.428 but failed to add them correctly. Their sum rounds to $2,223.39, not $4,412.33.

The model understated employee FICA by failing to apply the combined 7.65% Social Security and Medicare rate accurately to all $29,064 of wages. The two components are $1,801.97 and $421.43, totaling $2,223.39 rather than $2,090.

The model used the correct 7.65% FICA rate but rounded the resulting liability to $2,220 instead of calculating and reporting the required dollar amount. Applying 7.65% to $29,064 yields $2,223.396 before component-level cent rounding and $2,223.39 from the separately rounded Social Security and Medicare components.

The model incorrectly treated reaching full retirement age as an exemption from employee Social Security and Medicare taxes. Wages remain subject to FICA regardless of retirement age, producing $1,801.97 of Social Security tax and $421.43 of Medicare tax.

The model incorrectly bypassed the gross-income eligibility limit because both household members are elderly and proceeded directly to a speculative net-income calculation. It also treated the mortgage balance as though it established deductible shelter expenses, even though no rent, mortgage payment, property tax, insurance, or utility expense was listed; the $44,289 gross income instead fails the threshold and yields value = 0.

The model invented an aged Medicaid pathway based on the spouse having no individual income, even though the spouse qualifies through no non-MAGI category and receives no SSI. It also acknowledged that household MAGI exceeds the expansion limit but then replaced the required eligibility test with a generalization that PolicyEngine typically treats low-income aged spouses as eligible.

The model incorrectly declared the couple’s $44,289 income to be well below Virginia’s aged, blind, and disabled income limit and therefore assigned an ABD pathway that the spouse does not satisfy. Minimal countable resources cannot establish ABD eligibility when the applicable categorical and income requirements are unmet.

The model treated age 69 and unspecified household information as enough to establish Medicaid eligibility without applying any pathway. The actual pathway evaluation yields category NONE: MAGI is 2.05 times FPL and no non-MAGI category applies.

The model conflated eligibility for a Medicare Savings Program with Medicaid eligibility and asserted MSP receipt without applying Virginia’s income and categorical tests. Being Medicare-aged does not establish either MSP participation or a Medicaid eligibility category, and this spouse qualifies through none.

The model incorrectly treated 40 quarters of Medicare-covered employment as a prerequisite for Medicare eligibility rather than a condition for premium-free Part A. Under the requested PolicyEngine rule, the spouse's age of 69 satisfies the age-65 Medicare eligibility criterion, so the unlisted work history does not change the result.

The model allowed only $21,484 of total deductions and exemptions, omitting most of the two $12,000 Virginia age deductions available to this couple. Those age deductions, together with the joint standard deduction and personal exemptions, reduce Virginia taxable income to zero rather than $9,918.25.

The model applied an unspecified standard-deduction shortcut without accounting for the full Virginia age deductions for both spouses over 65. The combined age deductions, joint standard deduction, and personal exemptions eliminate taxable income, so no bracket tax remains.

The model incorrectly offset the head’s $12,000 Virginia age deduction by his $15,225 of Social Security benefits and consequently allowed an age deduction only for the spouse. Virginia’s income-based age-deduction calculation does not reduce the head’s deduction dollar-for-dollar by Social Security received here; both spouses’ deductions apply and eliminate taxable income.

Although the explanation names two age deductions, the submitted $250.20 necessarily leaves positive taxable income and therefore fails to apply the stated deductions in the computation. Excluding Social Security and subtracting both $12,000 age deductions, the joint standard deduction, and personal exemptions leaves zero Virginia taxable income.

The model substituted a $1,600 age-related addition for Virginia’s income-based age deductions of up to $12,000 per qualifying spouse. Applying the full age deductions for both spouses, rather than a small age addition, fully offsets Virginia taxable income.

The model included the household’s gross Social Security in Virginia income instead of removing Social Security and then produced mutually inconsistent taxable-income and bracket calculations. With Social Security excluded and both spouses’ age deductions plus the joint standard deduction and personal exemptions applied, Virginia taxable income is zero.

The model calculated the return as single or head-of-household, using the $25,000 and $34,000 Social Security thresholds and only the head's standard deduction despite the specified joint filing. Under the MFJ thresholds, only $4,390 of Social Security is taxable, and the joint standard deduction with two senior additions eliminates taxable income.

The model incorrectly included the $24,000 disability benefit in AGI, overstated taxable Social Security at $23,663 instead of $4,390, and used an undersized standard deduction plus personal exemptions. Correct AGI is $23,130, which is fully absorbed by the MFJ standard deduction with two senior additions.

The model treated the $24,000 disability benefit as taxable and overstated taxable Social Security at $23,663. Excluding disability and applying the MFJ Social Security formula produces $4,390 of taxable Social Security and $23,130 of AGI, below the applicable standard deduction.

The model included all $44,080 of Social Security in taxable income instead of applying the MFJ provisional-income formula. Only $4,390 is taxable, so AGI is $23,130 and the joint standard deduction with senior additions reduces taxable income to zero.

The model expressly included taxable disability and arrived at positive taxable income after deductions. The disability benefit is excluded, only $4,390 of Social Security is taxable, and the resulting $23,130 AGI is less than the joint standard deduction with two senior additions.

The model expressly treated disability income as taxable and computed positive joint taxable income. Excluding that benefit and limiting taxable Social Security to $4,390 yields $23,130 of AGI, which the applicable joint standard deduction fully offsets.

The model incorrectly included the $24,000 disability benefit and overstated taxable Social Security at $37,468 by applying the 85% regime even though MFJ provisional income is only $40,780, below the $44,000 upper threshold. The correct taxable Social Security amount is $4,390, producing $23,130 of AGI and no taxable income after the standard deduction.

The model included the $24,000 disability benefit in AGI and overstated taxable Social Security at $23,663. The correct amounts are zero taxable disability and $4,390 taxable Social Security, leaving $23,130 of AGI below the MFJ standard deduction with two senior additions.

Although the model ultimately excluded disability, it treated all $44,080 of Social Security as taxable merely because provisional income exceeded the first MFJ threshold. Provisional income of $40,780 remains below the $44,000 second threshold, making only $4,390 taxable; AGI is $23,130 and the joint standard deduction eliminates it.

The model correctly identified a zero taxable wage base and then contradicted that computation by inventing taxable wage-equivalent income and assigning $1,926 of Social Security and Medicare taxes. No listed income is employee compensation subject to payroll tax, so the employee Social Security, Medicare, Additional Medicare, and mandatory state payroll-tax components all equal zero.

The model incorrectly evaluated the spouse as a separate zero-income individual and assumed that age alone opened an aged Medicaid pathway. Washington's pathway evaluation includes the applicable household income and categorical requirements; this spouse receives no SSI, has household MAGI of 2.90 times FPL, and qualifies for no category.

The model's reasoning computes approximately $22,379 but submits $27,049, so its final value does not follow its own calculation. It also disallows the $1,118 traditional IRA deduction, leaving AGI $1,118 too high instead of $182,172.27.

The model deducts the nonexistent $23,926 traditional 401(k) deferral from zero wages, understates taxable Social Security by using 85% of benefits above $32,000 rather than the statutory provisional-income formula, and applies an age-65 deduction even though both spouses are under 65. Those errors severely understate taxable income and tax.

The model explicitly calculates tax near $22,652 but submits $19,524, a final-answer inconsistency unsupported by its work. It also rejects the $1,118 traditional IRA deduction included in the required $2,699.98 of above-the-line deductions.

The model rejects the $1,118 traditional IRA deduction and therefore uses AGI of $183,291 rather than $182,172.27. It also estimates the 2026 bracket thresholds instead of applying the required thresholds, producing $22,219 of ordinary tax rather than $21,590.70.

The model places too much income into the higher ordinary-rate brackets, reporting about $23,886 of ordinary tax when the 2026 joint-bracket calculation yields $21,590.70. It also omits the $1,118 traditional IRA deduction, overstating taxable income.

The model uses a guessed $30,000 standard deduction instead of $32,200 and rejects the $1,118 traditional IRA deduction. These choices raise ordinary taxable income to $149,531 rather than the required taxable-income derivation from AGI of $182,172.27.

The model reaches AGI and taxable income close to the required amounts but rounds the bracket calculation to $22,000 rather than computing it. Applying the exact 2026 brackets to $149,972.27 and adding $564 of preferential-rate tax yields $22,154.70.

The model incorrectly applies pre-TCJA personal exemptions and 10%/15%/25% ordinary brackets. The applicable computation uses a $32,200 joint standard deduction, no personal exemptions, and the 2026 10%/12%/22% brackets at this income level.

The model incorrectly substitutes a $16,000 standard deduction plus personal exemptions and applies pre-TCJA 10%/15%/25% brackets. The computation requires the single $32,200 joint standard deduction and current-law 2026 brackets.

The submitted explanation treats approximately $183,865 as taxable income even after claiming to account for deductions. Correct AGI is $182,172.27 and the $32,200 standard deduction reduces taxable income to $149,972.27.

The model assumes expiration of the governing rate and deduction structure, introduces personal exemptions, and applies the resulting pre-TCJA-style calculation. The required 2026 computation uses the $32,200 joint standard deduction and current-law brackets.

The model incorrectly uses a $16,100 standard deduction, $10,100 of personal exemptions, and post-sunset ordinary brackets. The required taxable income is $149,972.27 after a $32,200 standard deduction, with no personal exemptions.

The model uses a $30,800 joint standard deduction and omits the $1,118 traditional IRA deduction. The correct deductions produce AGI of $182,172.27 and taxable income of $149,972.27, lowering ordinary tax to $21,590.70.

The model introduces personal exemptions into the 2026 computation and uses an unspecified standard-deduction and rate structure that produces a pre-TCJA-style liability. The required calculation uses a $32,200 standard deduction, no personal exemptions, and current-law 2026 brackets.

The model incorrectly caps the actual $1,582 net capital loss as a $3,000 loss, invents a $500 sick-spouse credit, and uses the wrong deduction and rate schedule. Its submitted $49,523.45 also contradicts the $28,867 result stated in its own explanation.

The model invents age-65 and itemized deductions large enough to eliminate tax even though both spouses are under 65 and the listed medical costs do not clear the 7.5%-of-AGI floor. The actual deductions leave $149,972.27 of taxable income.

The model's $2,320 result implies that it removed most of the household's taxable retirement and Social Security income through unsupported deductions or credits. The listed income and permitted deductions instead produce $149,972.27 of taxable income and no identified nonrefundable credit reduction.

The model estimates taxable income at about $151,091, omitting the $1,118 traditional IRA deduction included above the line. Correct taxable income is $149,972.27, and the exact bracket-plus-preferential-rate calculation is $22,154.70.

The submitted amount tracks a calculation using taxable income near $151,090 rather than $149,972.27. The model omitted the $1,118 traditional IRA deduction and therefore overstated the ordinary-rate tax.

The model uses taxable income of about $151,091 because it omits the $1,118 traditional IRA deduction. Applying the full $2,699.98 above-the-line deduction gives taxable income of $149,972.27 and total tax of $22,154.70.

The model computes from taxable income of $151,090.50 rather than $149,972.27. The $1,118 traditional IRA contribution is deductible in the required computation and reduces the ordinary-rate portion accordingly.

The model treats contributions and deductions as sufficient to offset all retirement income, despite $94,720 of taxable IRA distributions, $32,525.29 of taxable pension income, and $50,583.25 of taxable Social Security. Permitted deductions leave $149,972.27 taxable, not zero.

The model assumes a post-TCJA sunset, applies a reduced standard deduction plus personal exemptions, and uses 10%/15%/25% brackets. The applicable calculation uses the $32,200 joint standard deduction, no personal exemptions, and current-law 2026 brackets.

The model applies a post-TCJA-sunset deduction and rate regime, including personal exemptions and 10%/15%/25% brackets. It also rejects the $1,118 traditional IRA deduction; the required calculation uses current-law brackets and AGI of $182,172.27.

The model uses inflation-adjusted pre-TCJA personal exemptions, a $17,103 standard deduction, and pre-TCJA ordinary brackets. The required 2026 calculation instead uses a $32,200 standard deduction, no personal exemptions, and current-law brackets.

The model overstates AGI at about $184,371 through an erroneous aggregation of the listed income and deductions. The trace yields gross income of $184,872.25, $2,699.98 of above-the-line deductions, AGI of $182,172.27, and taxable income of $149,972.27.

The model applies a projected pre-TCJA regime with a $16,950 standard deduction, personal exemptions, and 10%/15%/25% brackets. It also rejects the $1,118 traditional IRA deduction; the required computation uses the $32,200 standard deduction and current-law 2026 brackets.

The model invents a $500 car-loan-interest deduction and rejects the $1,118 traditional IRA deduction. The allowed above-the-line deductions total $2,699.98, and auto-loan interest is not part of this federal taxable-income derivation.

The model defaults to zero because wages are unlisted, ignoring the substantial taxable IRA distributions, pension income, Social Security, interest, and dividends. Those nonwage sources produce $149,972.27 of taxable income after the applicable deductions.

The model fails to deduct the $1,582 net capital loss and instead reports gross income as AGI, while also granting an age-based deduction to a 64-year-old. Its submitted $41,228.50 further contradicts the $25,531.98 tax calculated in its explanation.

The model supplies no supporting arithmetic for its $21,902.90 estimate. The required derivation produces $149,972.27 of taxable income, $21,590.70 of ordinary tax, and $564 of preferential-rate tax, so its answer understates the bracket calculation.

The model replaced current-year Medicare eligibility with an invented near-term eligibility rule. Being age 64 and approaching 65 does not satisfy the age-65 threshold during a year in which age is constant.

The reasoning correctly stated that the age-64 head is not Medicare eligible, but the model submitted value = 1, reversing its own eligibility conclusion. The required numeric encoding was 0 for “not eligible.”

The model invented a projection from age 64 to future age-65 eligibility. The benchmark holds age constant throughout 2026, and no disability or qualifying disease pathway is present, so the head fails every Medicare eligibility pathway.

The model invented a $10 hourly wage for both adults from their weekly hours even though hourly wage and wage income were unlisted and therefore zero under the prompt. It then applied Social Security and Medicare rates to fabricated annual wages, and its stated total also adds an unexplained $947.17 beyond its own $1,354.08 and $316.68 components.

The model annualized weekly hours into labor earnings without any listed hourly wage or wage amount. Weekly hours alone create no payroll-tax base; with unlisted wages set to zero, Social Security and Medicare employee taxes are both zero.

The model correctly identified that Texas has no general individual income tax, then invented a $280 “nonstandard component” unsupported by any Texas tax rule or household fact. It failed to carry the Texas zero through the 51-jurisdiction aggregation, whose components all equal zero because the household resides exclusively in Texas.

The model treated the full $51,475 of Social Security as gross income and then inconsistently asserted that about $36,571 was taxable, instead of applying the joint provisional-income test that excludes all of the benefits. It also produced $5,885 after its own bracket calculation yielded $3,280, so its submitted amount does not follow its stated arithmetic.

The model correctly derived zero taxable income from $1,065 of net non-Social-Security income and the joint standard deduction, then discarded that result by inventing unlisted wages from the adults' work hours. The prompt expressly sets unlisted numeric income to zero, so no wage income can support the submitted $4,600 liability.

The submitted $3,144 implies that the model included a taxable portion of Social Security or otherwise failed to let the joint standard deduction eliminate taxable income. The provisional-income calculation leaves Social Security nontaxable, and the remaining $1,065 is below the standard deduction.

The model correctly stated that no Social Security benefits enter taxable income, but then calculated taxable income as $52,540 minus the $30,950 standard deduction, thereby putting the excluded $51,475 back into the tax base. With Social Security excluded, only $1,065 remains before the standard deduction, yielding zero taxable income rather than $21,590.

The model computed MAGI as $1,065 by using $1,200 of taxable interest minus the $135 partnership loss and omitting the Social Security retirement income included in the Medicaid MAGI calculation. The resulting MAGI is approximately $52,540, or 2.39 times FPL, above the expansion-adult threshold, and the head qualifies through no other Medicaid category.

The model acknowledged the age-65 rule but invented an unspecified special-status pathway despite all unlisted statuses being false. At age 62 with no qualifying disability, end-stage renal disease, or ALS status, the head is not Medicare eligible.

The model's explanation computed Medicare eligibility as 0 under the age-65 rule but submitted value = 1. This is an internal answer-contract contradiction: its numeric output does not match its stated conclusion.

The model incorrectly treated receipt of Social Security retirement benefits at age 62 as conferring Medicare eligibility. Retirement-benefit receipt does not replace the age-65 requirement, and no qualifying disability, end-stage renal disease, or ALS pathway is present.

The model directly misapplied the age threshold by stating that age 62 meets a requirement of age 65 or older. Because 62 is below 65 and no non-age eligibility pathway is listed, the head is not Medicare eligible.

The model correctly stated that no wages were listed and that Social Security retirement income does not generate employee payroll tax, but then submitted $5,108 instead of the resulting $0. Its numeric answer applies payroll tax to a nonexistent or ineligible earnings base and directly contradicts its own derivation.

The model incorrectly assigned the spouse MAGI of $1,065 instead of using the tax-unit MAGI that places the spouse at 2.39 times FPL, evidently omitting the head's Social Security retirement and other relevant tax-unit income from the Medicaid MAGI computation. Because 2.39 times FPL exceeds the 138% expansion limit and the spouse qualifies through no categorical pathway, the spouse is not eligible.

The model treated $38,606 of Social Security as New York-taxable income instead of applying New York's subtraction for Social Security benefits. It also applied a percentage directly to an asserted taxable amount without correctly using New York's graduated bracket computation; excluding Social Security leaves only $1,065 before the standard deduction and zero taxable income.

After correctly deriving near-zero New York taxable income from the listed amounts, the model invented approximately $90,000 of wages from the spouses' work hours and median-wage assumptions. The prompt explicitly sets unlisted wage amounts to zero, so those imputed wages cannot enter New York taxable income.

The submitted $1,582 implies a positive New York taxable-income base, but the model gave no computation supporting one. New York's Social Security exclusion leaves $1,200 of interest minus the $135 partnership loss, and the joint standard deduction reduces that $1,065 remainder to zero.

The model began its state calculation with the full $51,475 Social Security benefit in federal AGI and then failed to remove it consistently when deriving its asserted $18,426 taxable income. It also incorrectly added back the $721 traditional IRA contribution; after New York's Social Security subtraction, the remaining $1,065 is below the joint standard deduction, producing zero taxable income.

The model substituted a guessed $32,600 standard deduction and omitted the traced $5,163.84 above-the-line deduction, producing $501,670 rather than $503,494.75 of taxable income. It also treated NIIT as outside the requested output, omitting $5,721.98.

The model invented roughly $110,000 of mortgage interest from the mortgage balance despite the instruction that unlisted expenses are zero, then produced a tax amount incompatible with its own stated taxable income. Employer insurance premiums are not nonrefundable income-tax credits or investment deductions.

The model explicitly excluded the $5,721.98 NIIT and then submitted $91,458 even though its own regular-tax components summed to about $102,907. The required components are $89,095.92 ordinary tax, $11,688 preferential tax, and $5,721.98 NIIT.

The model fabricated mortgage interest using an assumed 7% rate and an estimated $60,000 itemized deduction, contrary to the zero-for-unlisted-input rule. It also used a 20% qualified-dividend rate instead of the traced $11,688 tax on $77,920 at 15%.

The model arithmetically overstated AGI as about $604,318; the income items it listed yield $538,418 before the engine's further traced adjustments. It also invented roughly $60,000 of deductions from unlisted mortgage interest rather than applying the traced deductions.

The model applied an obsolete-law TCJA-sunset regime with pre-TCJA ordinary brackets, restored miscellaneous deductions, personal AMT parameters, and a speculative mortgage rate. The 2026 rules used by the trace yield $89,095.92 of ordinary-bracket tax and no added AMT component, followed by $11,688 of preferential tax and $5,721.98 of NIIT.

The model invented approximately $28,000 of mortgage interest from a balance with no listed interest expense and consequently used an unsupported $40,574 itemized deduction. The trace instead applies $33,269.77 of taxable-income deductions and produces $503,494.75 of taxable income.

The model replaced the regular-tax result with a $131,247 tentative AMT. The traced liability contains $89,095.92 of ordinary tax and $11,688 of preferential tax, with no AMT increment, plus $5,721.98 of NIIT.

The model incorrectly applied a TCJA-expiration framework with uncapped SALT, a mortgage-interest deduction on an assumed $1 million debt limit, and personal exemptions. Those rules reduced ordinary tax to $88,016 instead of the traced $89,095.92.

The model used an unsupported $460,936 AGI and described tax-exempt pension income as part of its income calculation. The trace starts from $541,928.34 of gross income, applies $5,163.84 above the line and $33,269.77 below the line, and taxes $503,494.75.

The model added an AMT component and used an unsupported AGI of roughly $525,049. The traced calculation has no AMT increment and totals only the $89,095.92 ordinary tax, $11,688 preferential tax, and $5,721.98 NIIT.

The model applied an expired-law framework with uncapped SALT and ordinary rates reaching 33%. The operative 2026 parameters and traced deductions produce $89,095.92 of ordinary tax, not the larger sunset-law estimate.

The model deducted $13,369 of employer-sponsored insurance premiums from wages even though the trace's employment-income reduction is the $41,650 of allowed pre-tax 401(k) contributions.
